1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and keeps both a solid central set-up and a fianchetto of the c8-bishop in reach. Black stays flexible and sound. The price is a c8-bishop hemmed in by the e6-pawn, which usually has to find its diagonal by a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and kingside castling, and keeps both a King's Indian and a Grünfeld set-up open. Black lets White build a centre first and plans to strike at it later with pawn breaks. The cost is that White has the first say in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Meets the pawn with a pawn and takes a share of the centre, which also lets the c8-bishop come out before ...e6. The game heads for classical queen's pawn structures. The cost is that White decides which structure arises.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to bear on e4 and the long diagonal, and keeps a solid pawn set-up in hand. Black controls the centre from a distance rather than occupying it. The cost is that the centre stays with White for now.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5.name: Indian Defence: Spielmann-Indian Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and heads for a Benoni-type structure, trading central space for queenside counterplay. It is less common than the main replies, and White, not obliged to play c4, can build a big centre and press with extra space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d6.name: Indian Defence: Tartakower Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Frees the c8-bishop and prepares to challenge the centre later, while several set-ups stay open. Sound but modest: the d6-pawn claims less space than ...d5, and White keeps a free choice of set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6.name: Indian Defence: Czech-Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid pawn chain and keeps other set-ups in reserve. White need not play c4, and the c6-pawn has taken the natural square of the b8-knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.name: Döry Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.background: The Döry Defence was the subject of a theme tournament in Vienna in 1937, won by Paul Keres. It is uncommon, and sometimes transposes into a variation of the Queen's Indian Defence.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight on a central post at once, to be supported later by pawn moves or a fianchetto of the c8-bishop. This knight has now moved twice, and White can challenge it with a knight to d2, aiming to trade it off or, after Nfd2, to drive it back with f3 and gain time for e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight but invites 3.d5, which attacks it at once. 3...Ne5 loses the piece to 4.Nxe5, so the knight goes back to b8 or to a5 or b4, where it is soon driven on, and White has gained space and time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for the centre. White can take space in the centre while the piece stays out of play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Rg8.strategy: Moves the rook for no purpose, wasting a tempo and giving up the right to castle kingside. No other piece is developed and the king has lost its natural shelter.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a6.name: Indian Defence: Knights Variation, Alburt-Miles Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares queenside expansion and loses little, since nothing threatens Black yet. But it spends a tempo on a rim pawn while the centre and development are untouched, so White builds the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Stops b4 and gains queenside space, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn and leaves the b5-square weak. Neither the centre nor development is addressed, so White simply builds the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b5.name: Indian Defence: Polish Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but spends a tempo on a pawn push with only one piece developed. The b5-pawn becomes a target: e3 or e4 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to it, and a4 or c4 attack it as well.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's bishop and loses little, since nothing threatens Black yet. But the pawn does nothing for the centre or development, so White gets a free tempo to build the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and g6 without developing anything. White takes the free tempo to build the centre, and the advanced h-pawn gains nothing in return.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ng8.strategy: Retreats the knight to where it began, undoing Black's first move. White gets two free tempi in the centre and can set up as it likes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time with no real threat, since the f3-knight and the h1-rook guard h2 and the king guards f2. 3.h3 drives it back, so Black has lost a tempo while White gains a useful move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where 3.g4 drives it back with gain of space; 3...Nf4 would lose it to 4.Bxf4. Black has spent two moves on the knight and developed nothing else.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but 3.c4 or 3.e4 drives it away with tempo, so that it moves a third time while White builds a broad pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Loses a pawn for little: the f3-knight and the d4-pawn both attack e5, and after 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 White is simply a pawn up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn, which both Nf3 and Bc1 attack and nothing defends, so 3.Bxg5 or 3.Nxg5 wins a pawn for nothing and leaves Black's kingside loosened.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5 3.d5.strategy: The usual reply: White gains space and cramps Black's centre instead of letting the c-pawn chip away at d4. The pawn on d5 is guarded only by the queen for now, so White has to support it, while Black plays against it with queenside play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5 3.c4.strategy: Keeps the pawn on d4 and adds the c-pawn's pressure on d5, steering towards a flexible, English-style game instead of the Benoni-like structure that 3.d5 creates. The cost is that the d4 pawn is challenged at once, so White has to be ready to recapture and fight for the d4 square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3.strategy: Shores up d4 and opens the king's bishop, keeping to the solid set-up White may have been heading for. It is less ambitious than 3.d5: Black can trade off the d4 pawn or pile up pressure on it, and White gives up the space that 3.d5 gains.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3.strategy: Starts the fianchetto before the centre is settled, and Black simply takes on d4. White has to recapture with the knight at once: 4.Bg2 lets ...e5 keep the pawn, since taking it loses the knight to ...Qa5+. Sound, but it gives up the space 3.d5 would gain.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4.strategy: Takes space on the queenside and puts the centre under pressure before Black's ...d5 arrives. The natural way to meet ...c6: White gets the bigger share of the centre, Black a solid structure to defend.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bf4.strategy: Brings the bishop out in front of the pawn chain before an e3 could shut it in, and avoids the theory that follows c4. White gets an easy development and a sound centre, while Black gets a comfortable structure and a free game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.e3.strategy: A modest, solid reply that supports d4 and opens the bishop's diagonal, but leaves the c1-bishop behind its own pawns for now. Black meets the centre at once and White gets no space advantage.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 b5.name: Slav Indian: Kudischewitsch Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 b5.background: Sometimes called the Kudischewitsch Gambit, after the Israeli IM David Kudischewitsch.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 b5.strategy: A pawn offer that challenges the c4 pawn at once to open the queenside. It loosens Black's own queenside, so Black has to show that the open lines are worth the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre at once and builds a sturdy chain of pawns on c6 and d5 that keeps the queenside bishop free to develop outside it. Black accepts a slight deficit in space for a solid structure, and the task is to finish development before White's centre grows.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid pawn chain, but locks in the queenside bishop for the time being. Black accepts a cramped yet sturdy position and puts off the decision about that bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4 d6.strategy: Holds the centre with a modest pawn and keeps the pieces flexible, aiming for a later central pawn break. Black gives White the space, and the game is a slow one in which White can build a broad centre that Black must undermine.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.c4.strategy: The principled move: the c-pawn adds to the grip on d5 and takes space, and White decides later what kind of game it will be. Black has to choose a set-up at once: occupy the centre, fight for e4 with a bishop, or fianchetto on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.name: Indian Defence: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.background: The London System takes its name from the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared seven times, in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein. James Mason had been the first master-level player to use it regularly, including at the Vienna tournament of 1882.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Puts the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before a pawn on e3 can shut it in, and eyes the e5 square. The set-up is solid, easy to learn and light on theory, but it asks little of Black, who can develop freely and challenge d4 with a pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.background: The Torre Attack is named after the Mexican grandmaster Carlos Torre Repetto, who beat the former world champion Emanuel Lasker with it. Tartakower, Spassky and, early in his career, Petrosian also played it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the f6 knight to the queen, so Black cannot use that knight freely. White aims for quick, quiet development and a later kingside attack; the price is that the bishop no longer covers b2 and can be harassed.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3.name: Yusupov-Rubinstein System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3.strategy: Supports the d4 pawn and opens the f1-bishop, the quiet way to build a sturdy centre. White keeps the plan open: a bishop on d3 and a well-timed e4 break, or the queen's bishop on the long diagonal. The cost is a c1-bishop hemmed in behind the pawns until the plan is chosen.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and watches e4 and d5, but blocks the c-pawn, so White gives up the space-gaining c4 push. Black can pin the knight against the king with the bishop or take the centre at once, and White is left with a sound position and no clear plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5.strategy: The most active answer: Black hits d4 before White's set-up gets going, and the bishop on g5 has not yet found a job. White must either support the centre quietly or sacrifice a pawn for activity. Black gets queenside space and a healthy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and reaches a solid structure in which White's bishop is already committed to g5. The f6 knight stays pinned to the queen until the dark-squared bishop breaks the pin. Safe and simple, but the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6 pawn for a long time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 h6.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop before Black has committed the centre: White must either keep the pin and risk a pawn attack on the bishop, or give it up for the knight. It costs a tempo and loosens the kingside a little, but it removes the bishop's sting early.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3.strategy: The solid reply: it defends d4 and opens the way for the f1-bishop, keeping the Torre set-up intact. White accepts that the bishop has left b2 without cover, so the b-pawn needs watching, and plays for a calm build-up and a kingside attack against Black's queenside space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e4.name: Torre Attack: Wagner Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e4.strategy: A sharp pawn break while the bishop pins the f6-knight. After 4...cxd4 5.e5 Black has to find the only move, ...h6, and the forcing play regains the pawn with a lively game. Sound, but it leaves the solid Torre set-up for a gamble.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.c3.strategy: Backs d4 with a pawn, so a capture there is met by a recapture that keeps the centre, and holds the e2-e4 break in reserve. White builds a firm centre first and can meet a queen sortie to b6, at the cost of a slower start for the king's bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will fight for the e4 square and the long diagonal from a distance. The pawn also keeps c5 well guarded. Black leaves the centre alone for now and bets on piece pressure against White's centre rather than on occupying space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 cxd4.strategy: Trades Black's c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the c-file. White keeps a central pawn after recapturing, so the game stays level, but the pin on f6 is still there and Black has a simple structure and clear targets to play against.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 Qb6.strategy: Sends the queen after the b2 pawn, which the departure of the c1-bishop left without a defender. It is a testing, double-edged choice: White gets time to develop against a queen away from the centre, and the pawn grab can cost Black more time than it earns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.d5.name: Torre Attack: Classical Defence, Petrosian Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.d5.strategy: Pushes past the c5-pawn to cramp Black while the bishop keeps f6 pinned. After 5...exd5 6.Nc3 the d5-pawn is attacked by queen and knight and defended only by the pinned f6-knight, so White wins it back and stands better; if Black declines, White has gained space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop to guard e4, the square the fianchettoed bishop will contest, keeps the pin on f6 and clears the way to castle. Sound and harmonious, but it plays for a quiet game where 5.d5 takes space at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.Nbd.strategy: Brings the last minor piece into play towards e4, the square both sides fight for, and keeps the pin on f6. Sound, but it does not yet put pressure on Black's kingside, so Black can complete development without difficulty.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 c5 4.e3 b6 5.c3.strategy: Props up d4 against the c-pawn and takes the c3 square from the queen's knight. Solid and harmless: it neither develops a piece nor builds pressure, and the extra pawn move lets Black reach an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, so White cannot build the centre in peace. Black gets queenside space and counterplay, and the central pawn structure is decided early: White must keep d4 supported or release the tension. The most direct way to meet the quiet set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, so Black fights for e4 from a distance instead of occupying the centre with pawns. It is flexible and comfortable, but it leaves White free to build the centre, and Black has to be ready to meet a later e4 break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and heads for a classical set-up. Black is solid and free of weaknesses, but the queen's bishop is shut in behind the e6 pawn, and White gets the quiet, harmonious development it aims for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop on the diagonal that points at h7 and prepares castling. It also stands guard over e4, the square White wants for a central break, and meets Black's long-diagonal bishop on the same battleground. A natural, harmonious step in the system.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.c4.strategy: Adds the c-pawn to the d-pawn so that the two together command the centre, and meets Black's fianchetto with space instead of a slow build-up. The game becomes a mainstream fight between White's central pawns and Black's pieces on the long diagonals.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.b3.strategy: Mirrors Black's set-up and prepares the queen's bishop for the long diagonal, though d4 blocks that diagonal for now. Sound but unambitious: White has no immediate pressure on the centre, and Black can equalise without effort.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3 Bb7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop bears down on e4 and the f3 knight, and Black decides the centre later. The two bishops now face each other over e4, which makes White's central break harder to carry out and leaves a flexible game for both sides.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, so the queen's bishop, once it reaches the long diagonal, and the c-pawn work together against White's centre instead of waiting for it to grow. White can release the tension, but Black gets active queenside play either way.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3 Be7.strategy: Develops the kingside bishop and prepares castling, a flexible and safe way to finish the set-up. It commits to nothing in the centre and does nothing to disturb White, who keeps the choice of how to build.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 b6 4.Bd3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn, but the pawn on d5 now blocks the diagonal of the queen's bishop, which was the point of the b6 pawn. Solid, yet Black ends up with a passive bishop and a set-up that fights against itself.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop behind a well-supported d4 pawn and aims it at the kingside. White prepares castling and keeps the e4 break in the background, letting Black choose how to deal with the tension on d4. The standard route into the Colle structures.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.c3.strategy: Protects d4 with a pawn, so a capture there is met by a recapture that keeps the centre, and steers the queen's knight to d2. Solid but slow: the pawn takes c3 from that knight and Black gets time to develop without being challenged.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop for the long diagonal while d4 stays guarded by the e-pawn and the knight. A flexible route that aims at a kingside attack, though without a pawn on c3 Black can resolve the tension in the centre on its own terms.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5.strategy: Black builds the classical centre and takes the e4 square away from White's central break, which the bishop on d3 was preparing. The cost is a hemmed-in c8-bishop behind the e6 pawn, but the structure is solid and the game turns on how White supports d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d4 beside the c-pawn, so White must keep two defenders there, and the bishop on d3 blocks the queen from adding a third. Black develops with pressure and commits no central pawn yet.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 b6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto so that the queen's bishop looks along the long diagonal instead of being locked behind the e6 pawn. Black keeps the centre flexible, but White can build a broad centre while Black's pieces aim at it from a distance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.background: The Colle System was popularised in the 1920s by the Belgian master Edgard Colle and developed further by George Koltanowski; each won several tournaments with it in the 1920s and 1930s.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.c3.strategy: The traditional set-up: the pawn backs d4 solidly and prepares a knight on d2 and a central break on e4. White trades some activity for a safe centre, and the c1-bishop stays shut in behind the pawns. A sound, low-risk system with a simple plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.b3.name: Rubinstein Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.b3.strategy: Opens the long diagonal for the queen's bishop instead of shutting it in behind a pawn on c3, aiming for a kingside attack behind a modest-looking set-up. The cost is a d4 pawn with no c3 pawn behind it, and the c-pawn stays free for a later strike.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and adds a second defender of e4 before the central break, while the c-pawn stays free to go to c3 or c4. A sound move order, but it leaves Black free to resolve the tension on d4 first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3 c5 4.Bd3 d5 5.b3.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4: with the c5 pawn, Black attacks it twice, and White has to keep guarding it. Black stakes out the queenside and prepares quick castling, challenging White's quiet set-up to show a real plan.

Develops the bishop to its most active square, aimed at h2, the pawn in front of White's future castled king, and keeps the knight's development flexible. The bishop supports a central advance, and Black prepares to castle behind a harmonious set-up.
Clears the c-pawn from the centre and opens the c-file. White recaptures with a central pawn, so the game stays level, but Black develops easily and gets a clear target in the pawn on d4.

Secures the king before the centre is settled, so the bishop on d3 can aim at the kingside in earnest. White is ready to bring the queen's bishop to the long diagonal, and the plan is a slow build-up for a kingside attack, not an immediate fight for the centre.

Places the queen's bishop on the long diagonal at once, behind the d4 pawn, where it supports the kingside build-up. Castling can follow, but Black gets a moment to strike at the centre before White's king is safe.

Gives up the d4 pawn to open the long diagonal, but Black recaptures with a developing move and the bishop lands on an active square, eyeing the e3 pawn. White trades its central pawn for a wing pawn and gets little for it.

The most active square: the bishop looks at White's kingside along the diagonal to h2 and supports a later central advance, while Black's king gets ready to castle. Black has a harmonious, well-placed army against the attack.

The more modest square: the bishop stays behind the pawns and shields the king. It is solid and safe against a kingside attack, but it does less than a bishop on d6 and leaves Black passively placed if White gets the long diagonal working.

Trades Black's c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the c-file. The game stays level, and the pawn that recaptures on d4 becomes a target for Black's pieces, but Black gives up the tension that kept White's centre under pressure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once. With White's knight already on c3 and no c-pawn push to attack d5, the pawn is only hit by a knight and stands securely. Black gets the classical solid structure, and White must find a plan without the usual space gain.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3 knight to the king, since the d2 square is empty, and so makes White's e-pawn advance harder. Black can double White's pawns by taking on c3 whenever it suits, while White can break the pin by developing a bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Attacks d4 at once, but White's knight on c3 already watches d5 and e4, so White keeps the choice between pushing the d-pawn and building quietly. Playable, but Black gets no more than after the classical centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Veresov Attack, Classical Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.strategy: The natural way to develop the dark bishop outside the pawn chain, pinning the f6 knight to the queen so that Black's centre is harder to support. Black has simple ways to break the pin, so the pressure is mild, but White gets a comfortable, flexible game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.strategy: Develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, where it controls e5 and keeps the structure compact. It asks Black no immediate question, so Black develops freely and the game stays level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3.strategy: A modest move that opens the king's bishop and supports d4, building a compact centre. Sound, but it shuts in the c1-bishop and gives Black time to finish development without trouble.
